verses.text: Hezekiah sent to all Israel and Judah, and wrote letters also to Ephraim and Manasseh, that they should come to Yahweh’s house at Jerusalem, to keep the Passover to Yahweh, the God of Israel.
For the king had taken counsel with his princes and all the assembly in Jerusalem to keep the Passover in the second month.
For they could not keep it at that time, because the priests had not sanctified themselves in sufficient number, and the people had not gathered themselves together to Jerusalem.
The thing was right in the eyes of the king and of all the assembly.

So they established a decree to make proclamation throughout all Israel, from Beersheba even to Dan, that they should come to keep the Passover to Yahweh, the God of Israel, at Jerusalem, for they had not kept it in great numbers in the way it is written.

So the couriers went with the letters from the king and his princes throughout all Israel and Judah, and according to the commandment of the king, saying, “You children of Israel, turn again to Yahweh, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, that he may return to the remnant of you that have escaped out of the hand of the kings of Assyria.
Don’t be like your fathers and like your brothers, who trespassed against Yahweh, the God of their fathers, so that he gave them up to desolation, as you see.

Now don’t be stiff-necked, as your fathers were, but yield yourselves to Yahweh, and enter into his sanctuary, which he has sanctified forever, and serve Yahweh your God, that his fierce anger may turn away from you.

For if you turn again to Yahweh, your brothers and your children will find compassion before those who led them captive, and will come again into this land, because Yahweh your God is gracious and merciful, and will not turn away his face from you, if you return to him.”
So the couriers passed from city to city through the country of Ephraim and Manasseh, even to Zebulun, but people ridiculed them and mocked them.
Nevertheless some men of Asher and Manasseh and of Zebulun humbled themselves, and came to Jerusalem.
Also the hand of God came on Judah to give them one heart, to do the commandment of the king and of the princes by Yahweh’s word.
Many people assembled at Jerusalem to keep the feast of unleavened bread in the second month, a very great assembly.
They arose and took away the altars that were in Jerusalem, and they took away all the altars for incense and threw them into the brook Kidron.
Then they killed the Passover on the fourteenth day of the second month. The priests and the Levites were ashamed, and sanctified themselves, and brought burnt offerings into Yahweh’s house.
They stood in their place after their order, according to the law of Moses the man of God. The priests sprinkled the blood which they received of the hand of the Levites.
For there were many in the assembly who had not sanctified themselves: therefore the Levites were in charge of killing the Passovers for everyone who was not clean, to sanctify them to Yahweh.

For a multitude of the people, even many of Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun, had not cleansed themselves, yet they ate the Passover other than the way it is written. For Hezekiah had prayed for them, saying, “May the good Yahweh pardon everyone
who sets his heart to seek God, Yahweh, the God of his fathers, even if they aren’t clean according to the purification of the sanctuary.”
Yahweh listened to Hezekiah, and healed the people.

The children of Israel who were present at Jerusalem kept the feast of unleavened bread seven days with great gladness. The Levites and the priests praised Yahweh day by day, singing with loud instruments to Yahweh.

Hezekiah spoke encouragingly to all the Levites who had good understanding in the service of Yahweh. So they ate throughout the feast for the seven days, offering sacrifices of peace offerings, and making confession to Yahweh, the God of their fathers.
The whole assembly took counsel to keep another seven days, and they kept another seven days with gladness.

For Hezekiah king of Judah gave to the assembly for offerings one thousand bulls and seven thousand sheep; and the princes gave to the assembly a thousand bulls and ten thousand sheep: and a great number of priests sanctified themselves.
All the assembly of Judah, with the priests and the Levites, and all the assembly who came out of Israel, and the foreigners who came out of the land of Israel, and who lived in Judah, rejoiced.
So there was great joy in Jerusalem; for since the time of Solomon the son of David king of Israel there was nothing like this in Jerusalem.
Then the priests the Levites arose and blessed the people. Their voice was heard, and their prayer came up to his holy habitation, even to heaven.

footnotes.content: Hezekiah didn't just heal Judah—he reached across the broken divide to Israel too, inviting the northern kingdom to Jerusalem. When the Lord stirs up a king's heart toward unity, he writes letters to go where his voice alone cannot reach.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice the counsel—not just the king deciding alone, but taking princes and assembly into the thought. A leader who gathers wisdom often finds that others help him see what the Lord is stirring.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priests weren't ready; the people hadn't gathered. Yet Hezekiah didn't shame them into obedience—he found a way forward by moving to the second month. Flexibility in timing can be wisdom, not wavering.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When a thing seems right to both king and people, it's worth watching. The Lord often confirms direction when leadership and assembly move in one accord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Beersheba to Dan—the whole map of the old kingdom, from south to north. Hezekiah's couriers carried one message: come home to what was written. The Lord's word holds the boundary of our belonging.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You children of Israel, turn again." Not an angry summons, but a tender call back to Abraham's God. The remnant that escaped Assyria's hand could yet remember Whom their fathers knew.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The past speaks—not to condemn, but to warn. Fathers and brothers had turned away and saw desolation follow. But this warning is also an opening: you need not repeat their path.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Don't be stiff-necked"—the very hardness that had grieved the Lord before. To yield is to loosen your grip, to enter His sanctuary, to let His fierce anger turn to peace. The Lord's sanctuary stands ready, sanctified forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He promises more than pardon—He promises return. Your children will find mercy, your captivity will reverse, because He is gracious and will not hide His face. This is the heart of the Lord laid bare.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The couriers passed through and were mocked and ridiculed. Not every city heard the invitation gladly. But the Lord sends His word anyway, knowing that some hearts will bend.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From Asher, Manasseh, Zebulun—the north answered. "Some men humbled themselves" and came. The remnant who heard and obeyed became proof that the Lord's call still reaches broken people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The hand of God came on Judah—a mysterious gift of singleness of heart. Not forced compliance, but the Lord working within to unite them around His word. This is how real obedience begins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A very great assembly gathered for the feast—not just the few, but many people converging on Jerusalem. When the Lord stirs a return, He draws more than we dared hope.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They took away the altars—the false shrines—and threw them into the brook Kidron. The stream carries away what should not stand. Before feasting at the true altar, they cleared away the counterfeit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priests were ashamed and sanctified themselves. What a turning—shame that leads not to despair but to washing, to drawing near. The burnt offerings followed. Shame, when it opens the heart, is a path homeward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They stood in their order according to the law of Moses. The old way, the written way, held steady. When worship returns to its appointed order, you feel the weight of centuries of faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Many had not sanctified themselves, so the Levites did the work for them—killing the Passovers to sanctify. The Lord made a way even for the unclean who came with honest hearts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They ate the Passover not quite as written, yet Hezekiah had already prayed: "May the good Yahweh pardon everyone." He knew what was about to happen—that the Lord sees the heart reaching, even when the form falls short.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Who sets his heart to seek God." Not perfect compliance with ritual, but the heart turned toward Him. The Lord reads what matters most—the seeking, the reaching, the yearning to know Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh listened to Hezekiah, and healed the people. One prayer, heard; one king's intercession; and healing flowed. This is the power of standing between God and His people with a shepherd's heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven days of great gladness, with the Levites and priests praising day by day with loud instruments. The worship rose so high that heaven heard it. This is what the Lord's house sounds like when hearts truly return.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hezekiah spoke encouragement to the Levites who had good understanding. A leader who recognizes and affirms the faithful—those with skill in serving the Lord—multiplies their faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They took counsel to keep another seven days, and gladly did so. The joy became its own proof—why stop when the Lord is pouring out His favor? The feast overflowed its appointed time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hezekiah gave a thousand bulls, the princes gave thousands more, and the priests sanctified themselves in great numbers. The gifts flowed from the king down through the assembly—generosity breeding generosity, sanctification spreading like light.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah, Israel, priests, Levites, foreigners—all rejoiced together. The Lord gathered not just His people, but the stranger within the gates. His joy knows no boundary of tribe or origin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Since Solomon's time, nothing like this—such great joy in Jerusalem. The kingdom fragmented, then scattered, yet here gathered again in gladness. The Lord had knit back what seemed torn forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priests and Levites blessed the people, their voices heard, their prayer rising to heaven. Readers today hear an echo of this: when the Lord's people gather, their prayers ascend like incense, and blessing falls. He still listens when His priests intercede.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
